A retrieval system fails quietly when its embedding model changes but its stored vectors do not. The new query vectors occupy a different semantic geometry, so nearest-neighbor results become less meaningful even though latency stays flat. Re-embedding the corpus and measuring recall against a fixed relevance set makes that migration visible.

Start by naming the invariant that must remain true. For this system, that means deciding what result a user or operator must be able to trust before discussing implementation details. A clear invariant prevents the team from optimizing a nearby metric while the original failure remains possible. It also gives reviewers a short statement against which they can evaluate every later tradeoff.

Next, collect a baseline from normal production-shaped work. The baseline should record the outcome, the relevant latency or cost, and the conditions under which it was observed. Without that reference point, an apparent improvement can be nothing more than a change in traffic, data shape, or test environment. Evidence has value only when the comparison is like for like.

Then isolate the mechanism that connects the observed symptom to its proposed cause. A diagram or trace can help, but the useful output is a testable statement: when this condition changes, this part of the workflow should change in a predictable direction. That statement distinguishes causal reasoning from a list of facts that happen to be related to the same technology.

The control should be narrow enough to act on that mechanism. Broad remediation creates uncertainty because many unrelated changes can mask the result. A small change, applied behind a reversible boundary where possible, makes it easier to tell whether the intervention solved the stated problem. Reversibility is valuable because it protects the system while the evidence is still incomplete.

Define success before the rollout begins. The measure should reflect the original claim and include a threshold, a comparison period, and an owner who can interpret exceptions. A graph without a decision rule invites post-hoc explanation. A predeclared rule lets the team decide whether to continue, roll back, or investigate based on the same standard it used to justify the change.

Also name the failure mode that the proposed control does not address. Every mechanism has a boundary, and hiding that boundary turns a focused recommendation into an inflated promise. For example, a change that improves throughput may not improve correctness, and a change that improves correctness may increase latency. Stating the limit keeps the conclusion accurate and guides the next layer of work.

Most GPU inference bottlenecks are caused by moving weights, not multiplying matrices. A model with low arithmetic intensity spends more time waiting on memory bandwidth than on computation. Quantizing weights can help because smaller tensors reduce that transfer cost, provided accuracy remains within the product threshold.
